questions.text:
Maia's Dance Academy purchased new audio and lighting equipment costing $12,000 excluding GST. The wiring and installation costs totalled $1,200 excluding GST. Annual maintenance on the equipment is $350 excluding GST.

How will the new equipment be reported in the Statement of Financial Position? Use the concept of capital expenditure to justify the classification and dollar amount.
questions.expectedAnswer: Reported as non-current asset (PPE) at $13,200 ($12,000 + $1,200 wiring/installation). Maintenance is an ongoing operating expense, not capital expenditure.
questions.markingGuide: A: Reports as non-current asset. M: Explains capital expenditure concept — costs to acquire and install. E: Justifies exclusion of maintenance as ongoing operating cost.

questions.text:
Maia's Dance Academy received an invoice from Stage Lighting Services for studio lighting repairs.

Why does recording this invoice increase Maia's liabilities? Justify your answer by explaining how accounts payable meets all the characteristics of a liability and the recognition criteria.
questions.expectedAnswer: Liability characteristics: (1) present obligation from a past event (receiving the lighting repair service), (2) expected to result in an outflow of economic benefits (payment required), (3) amount can be reliably measured (invoice amount). Recognition criteria: probable outflow of economic benefits and reliable measurement are met.
questions.markingGuide: A: Identifies AP as liability. M: Explains characteristics — present obligation, past event, probable outflow, reliable measurement. E: Links to recognition criteria.

questions.text:
Maia's Dance Academy has two enrolment options:
- Casual class pass: $25 per class
- Term enrolment (10 weeks): $200 upfront (a 20% discount)

The accountant reports all class fees as one revenue line item in the Income Statement.

Using the concept of materiality, justify whether this reporting approach negatively impacts Maia's decision-making.
questions.expectedAnswer: Materiality: information is material if omitting or misstating it could influence decisions. Reporting as one total is acceptable if the breakdown would not change Maia's decisions. However, separating the two streams could help Maia understand which option is more popular, aiding pricing and scheduling decisions.
questions.markingGuide: A: Defines materiality. M: Applies to scenario. E: Discusses how breakdown could/could not influence decisions.

questions.text:
MAIA'S DANCE ACADEMY — ENROLMENT PACKAGES:
6 months @ $180/month | 12 months @ $160/month | 24 months @ $140/month
All memberships paid monthly, one month in advance.

Explain how this advertisement illustrates the concept of going concern for Maia's Dance Academy.
questions.expectedAnswer: Going concern assumes the entity will continue operating into the foreseeable future. Offering 12 and 24-month packages demonstrates Maia expects the business to operate for at least two more years. This assumption affects financial reporting — assets are reported at historical cost rather than liquidation value.
questions.markingGuide: A: Defines going concern. M: Links to long-term enrolment packages indicating continued operation. E: Discusses implications for financial reporting.

questions.text:
To promote the business, Maia ordered twelve branded water bottles at $20 each. In November, she gave eight to students who won a dance competition as prizes, gave two to her flatmates, and kept two for herself.

Discuss how these water bottles will be reported in the Income Statement and Statement of Financial Position. In your answer explain the accounting entity concept and the characteristics of an expense.
questions.expectedAnswer: Entity concept: the business is separate from the owner. The 8 given as prizes ($160) are a business expense (marketing/promotion). The 2 given to flatmates and 2 kept by Maia ($80) are drawings — personal use by the owner, not a business expense. An expense must: decrease economic benefits, occur during the reporting period, and result in a decrease in equity other than owner withdrawals.
questions.markingGuide: A: Identifies some as expense, some as drawings. M: Applies entity concept. E: Fully explains expense characteristics and correct treatment of all 12 bottles.

questions.text:
The chart below shows key financial figures from Maia's Dance Academy's Income Statement for the years ending 31 March 2023 and 2024.

Using the data from the chart, calculate the percentage change in profit from 2023 to 2024. Comment on the financial performance.
questions.expectedAnswer: Reporting period: both years cover 12 months to 31 March, making comparison valid. Comparability: same accounting policies used in both years enable meaningful comparison. Revenue increased by $33,000 (16.9%) and profit by $13,000 (39.4%). Since profit is growing faster than expenses, the business is becoming more profitable. Maia may decide not to raise fees since profitability is already improving.
questions.markingGuide: A: Identifies reporting period and comparability. M: Applies to data. E: Discusses decision implications with specific figures.

questions.text:
A local corporate client books weekly dance fitness classes for their staff. They are invoiced monthly. An allowance for doubtful debts is 3% of accounts receivable.

Note 1. Accounts receivable:
| Accounts receivable | 4,200 | |
| Less: Allowance for doubtful debts | (126) | 4,074 |

Justify how Note 1 aids Maia in decision-making. In your answer explain faithful representation, predictive value, and one limitation.
questions.expectedAnswer: Faithful representation: Note shows the true amount expected to be collected ($4,074), complete and free from bias. Predictive value: the allowance helps predict future cash flows — Maia can expect to collect about $4,074, not $4,200. Limitation: the 3% estimate is based on past experience and may not reflect future bad debts, especially if the corporate client's financial situation changes.
questions.markingGuide: A: Identifies faithful representation. M: Explains predictive value with context. E: Discusses limitation of estimation.
